content: Biotin is a vitamin that has received FDA approval for its role in strengthening hair follicles and preventing hair loss. It serves as a nutrient for the hair root, aiding in oxygenation and slowing hair loss. Additionally, it enhances the resilience and resistance of hair. Common adverse reactions associated with biotin include gastrointestinal upset. It is important to note that the administration of anticonvulsant medications may impair the absorption of biotin. For adults, biotin is a key component in formulations designed to strengthen hair follicles and prevent hair loss. It is recommended to apply the product to the hair follicle and massage until absorbed, with usage advised every 12 hours for optimal and sustained effects. Biotin is suitable for children, adolescents, adults, and seniors. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for oral biotin is 30 to 100 micrograms daily. For vaginal candidiasis, an oral dose of 20 milligrams daily is suggested. However, there is limited information regarding off-label, non-guideline-supported uses of biotin in adult patients. In pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding FDA-labeled uses of biotin. For partial biotinidase deficiency, a daily dose of 5 to 10 milligrams (or less) in solution or tablet form is recommended, with 9 milligrams daily administered in three divided doses. There is also limited information regarding off-label, non-guideline-supported uses of biotin in pediatric patients. Biotin is contraindicated in individuals with hypersensitivity to the vitamin. This product is intended for topical application only. If it comes into contact with the eyes, rinse immediately with water and consult a doctor. Adverse reactions reported include gastrointestinal upset. The use of anticonvulsant medications may impair biotin absorption. There is limited information available regarding clinical trial experiences, drug interactions, and monitoring of biotin. Regarding specific populations, there is no FDA guidance on the use of biotin during pregnancy, labor and delivery, or in nursing mothers. Similarly, there is no FDA guidance on its use in pediatric, geriatric, gender-specific, or racial populations, nor in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. There is also no guidance on its use in women of reproductive potential, males, or immunocompromised patients. Biotin is administered orally, but there is limited information regarding its monitoring, IV compatibility, and chronic overdose. The mechanism of action, structure, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of biotin are not well-documented in the drug label. Clinical studies on biotin are also limited. Storage information for biotin is not provided in the drug label. There is limited information regarding patient counseling and alcohol interactions with biotin. Patients are advised to consult their doctor about the effects of alcohol when taking this medication. Biotin is marketed under the brand name BIONA-VIT®. There is limited information regarding look-alike drug names for biotin.
